subject: Banking
title: How Banks Use Leverage
description: A fast breakdown of How Banks Use Leverage for builders.

hook.text: Banks hold $10-12 in assets for every $1 of their own money.

buildup.text: A 1% return on $1 trillion in assets equals $10 billion.

discovery.text: Leverage is why banking seems so profitable. Small margins on borrowed money create big returns for shareholders.

twist.text: Leverage also means a 10% loss in asset values wipes out all equity.

climax.text: Leverage makes banking the world's most rewarding and most dangerous business.

punchline.text: $10 borrowed for every $1 owned. Leverage makes banks rich and fragile.

quiz.question: What does 10:1 leverage mean for a bank?
options: The bank holds $10 in assets for every $1 of its own capital

details.summary: Banks use leverage by lending out many times more money than they hold in capital, amplifying both profits and losses. A bank with $10 billion in capital might hold $100 billion in assets, meaning a 10 percent loss on assets would wipe out all capital.
details.whyItMatters: Leverage is why banks are both extremely profitable and extremely fragile. It explains how small asset losses can destroy a bank's capital and why regulators obsess over capital ratios and stress tests.
takeaways: Large banks typically operate with 10:1 to 12:1 leverage ratios
Leverage amplifies returns on equity but also amplifies losses
Pre-2008 investment banks operated at leverage ratios of 30:1 or higher

faq.question: How does leverage make banks profitable?
faq.answer: If a bank earns 1% on $100 billion in assets but has only $10 billion in capital, that 1% return translates to a 10% return on equity. Leverage multiplies modest asset returns into attractive shareholder returns.

faq.question: Why don't regulators require banks to use less leverage?
faq.answer: Higher capital requirements make banks safer but reduce their return on equity and lending capacity. Regulators balance stability against economic output, and banks lobby intensely against capital rules that would reduce their leverage and profitability.
